newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico 28-day Cetes rate seen not bottoming yet.
newsitem.headline: Mexico 28-day Cetes rate seen not bottoming yet.

text.p: Mexican 28-day Cetes rates continued to test lower levels on Tuesday, defying expectations that they would inch higher, and analysts said the stable peso may enable help them dip a little further.
"I think there's still a little more room. It still hasn't hit the low of the fourth quarter last year," said Sonia Stromeyer, economist at MMS International in New York.

In Tuesday's auction, returns on the benchmark 28-day Treasury issue eased five basis points to 22.93 percent, the fifth consecutive week of declines that sent them plummeting from highs of 27.37 percent on Dec. 17.

In a Reuters poll on Tuesday, dealers had expected benchmark rates to rise to 23.03 percent. Analysts said the auction may have been favorably influenced by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, who gave no hints of a U.S. rate rise in a speech to the Senate Budget Committee on Tuesday.
The stable peso has also helped fuel the declines, as well as outlooks for steadily improving inflation.

Stromeyer said Cetes rates could edge below the floor of 22.74 percent achieved on Oct. 8, 1996 during the last cycle of declines. "Each time the cycle dips lower, because each time we're in a better inflation rate environment."
On Thursday, Banco de Mexico is due to release inflation data for the first 15 days of January, and a Reuters survey of economists has an average forecast of 1.24 percent.
"I think we shall receive something of a suprise in that the inflation bubble of December has begun to burst," said Gray Newman, an economist at HSBC James Capel.
He said the peso, which has unexpectedly strengthened against the dollar throughout the first weeks of the year, was also bolstering the confidence of investors.

"Most probably, the way this year is turning out, interest rates have room to keep on falling because of a more stable peso and a better panorama in everything related to debt service and industrial growth," said Francisco Gutierrez, an analyst at Inverlat brokerage in Mexico.
Foreign money has poured into Mexican markets and was fanned last week by the pre-payment of $5 billion in loans to the U.S. Treasury and the International Monetary Fund.
Rates on 91- and 182-day Cetes fell 27 and five basis points, respectively, to 24.16 percent and 24.63 percent.

At one point last year they rose slightly, but analysts said that may have been an aberration due to the different number of days in the maturity. The 342-day Cetes rate was 25.86 percent compared with 25.54 percent for the 349-day paper last week.
Demand in the auction dipped to 12.72 billion pesos from 13.80 billion last week, but the bid-to-cover ratio remained a healthy 3.85.
